summary:
I developed an interactive 3D web simulator, built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js, that evaluates the feasibility of landing missions and establishing permanent bases on the Moon, Mars, and four terrestrial analogues (Atacama, Death Valley, Haughton, and Villa de Leyva).

How does it address the challenge? The tool uses real NASA scientific data to transform critical variables (radiation, slope, dust, temperature, and communication delay) into an immersive experience. The user adjusts these conditions through an intuitive interface that calculates a "feasibility score" and determines whether the landing window is optimal. Subsequently, the rocket descent is simulated, unlocking a first-person (FPS) exploration mode with dynamic weather and procedural textures, allowing users to experience the environmental challenges up close.

Why is it important? The project democratizes access to the complexity of space exploration, serving as a powerful educational and scientific visualization tool to understand the environmental risks astronauts will face in future missions.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?
The simulator is an interactive 3D web application that works in two phases. First, users select a destination (Moon, Mars, or a terrestrial analogue) and adjust environmental variables like wind, dust, slope, and radiation. The system processes these inputs to calculate a real-time feasibility score and determines if the landing window is optimal. Second, it simulates a 3D rocket descent. Upon landing, users unlock a First-Person (FPS) exploration mode to walk on the surface, experiencing dynamic weather changes and procedural terrains.

2. What benefits does it offer?
It provides a risk-free, cost-effective environment to test mission parameters. It calculates EVA (Extravehicular Activity) factors, communication delays, and base feasibility, helping users understand the extreme conditions of space before committing to real-world mission designs.

3. What is the expected impact of the project?
The project aims to democratize space exploration education. It serves as a powerful scientific visualization tool that bridges the gap between complex NASA datasets and public understanding, inspiring the next generation of scientists and engineers by making planetary exploration accessible and engaging.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6 modules).
  • Libraries: Three.js for 3D rendering and WebGL.
  • Software: Developed using Sublime Text / Visual Studio Code, tested locally via a Python HTTP server.
  • Hardware: Standard computer hardware (runs directly in the web browser without high-end GPU requirements).

5. In what sense is your project creative?
The creativity lies in the integration of raw, complex NASA scientific data (like radiation levels and gravity) into a gamified, immersive experience. The use of procedural texture generation ensures that every environment feels unique, while the dynamic weather system (simulating Martian dust storms or Arctic fog) makes the simulation feel alive. The UI is also creatively designed to be collapsible, keeping the screen clean and avoiding visual clutter.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Accuracy: Grounding all data in verified NASA sources (LRO, MOLA) and scientific papers (McKay et al. 2003).
  • User Experience (UX): Designing an intuitive interface that doesn't overwhelm the user with data, using collapsible panels and clear HUD elements.
  • Performance: Optimizing the procedural terrain and particle systems so it runs smoothly in a standard web browser.
  • Accessibility: Making a complex aerospace concept understandable and interactive for students and enthusiasts without requiring specialized software.
